analysis.one_liner: Lets the Energy Department block EPA energy rules estimated to cost over $1 billion.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without ever getting a vote, so EPA's authority to issue energy-related rules was untouched.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA, before finalizing any energy-related rule estimated to cost more than $1 billion, to report its costs, benefits, energy-price effects, and job effects to Congress. It would then have handed the Department of Energy the power to block any such rule it determined would cause 'significant adverse effects to the economy.' In practice, that would have let one agency stop the EPA's biggest air and carbon pollution rules for power plants and other energy users.
analysis.who_benefits: Fossil fuel producers and other energy users facing expensive EPA rules would gain the most, because a $1 billion price tag plus any determination of higher energy prices, reduced fuel diversity, or reliability impact could trigger a block. Electricity consumers would see the reporting requirements as a check on price-increasing rules, and the bill would have given manufacturers and utilities a new lever to challenge costly regulations through the Energy Department.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fossil fuel producers and large energy users

how_it_helps.text: Before finalizing any EPA energy rule estimated to cost over $1 billion, the EPA would have to report to Congress the rule's total costs and benefits, estimated increases in gasoline or electricity prices for consumers, and detailed employment effects including potential job losses [S2] [S3].

The Energy Secretary, consulting FERC and the Energy Information Administration, would have to independently analyze whether the rule raises consumer energy prices, including for low-income households, small businesses, and manufacturers, or affects electricity reliability and fuel diversity [S3].

If the Secretary finds such an impact, the EPA would be flatly prohibited from finalizing the rule if the Secretary determines it will cause significant adverse effects to the economy — a veto power that overrides any other provision of law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall on people breathing pollution from power plants and other energy facilities, since rules whose health and environmental benefits exceed their costs could still be blocked if estimated costs top $1 billion and prices rise. The EPA's ability to carry out air and carbon pollution control would be curtailed, and communities bearing the health effects would have no equivalent veto over the outcome.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public health and EPA's clean-air authority

drawbacks.text: The bill's veto trigger is based on cost and energy-price effects, not on whether the rule's benefits outweigh its costs — a rule with large health benefits (such as avoided premature deaths) could still be blocked once its estimated costs passed $1 billion and prices were projected to rise [S3].

It would move the final decision on EPA pollution rules from the agency with environmental and health expertise to the Department of Energy, and a single adverse determination would kill a rule outright rather than prompting revisions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The reporting and independent price-impact analysis would give Congress and the public a clearer picture of what major energy rules cost consumers, which has genuine value. But the centerpiece is the Energy Department's veto over EPA rules, which is tilted toward stopping regulation: cost estimates and projected price increases alone could sink a rule whose health benefits dwarf its costs. On balance, the bill would do more to shield energy producers and heavy energy users from regulation than to protect ordinary households.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Heller introduced the bill on July 25, 2013, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1] [S5].
The bill attracted two Republican cosponsors and no further action; the committee never reported it and the full Senate never voted on it before the 113th Congress ended [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, EPA kept its existing authority to issue energy-related pollution rules, and the public retained the health protections those rules provide. Fossil fuel producers and other energy interests did not get the veto mechanism they would have gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA's regulatory authority and public health protections

for.name: Sen. Dean Heller
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled action, markup, or a floor report, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican with two Republican cosponsors and never reached a vote, so no roll call shows how the parties lined up.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers
industries.note: The bill would have given them a mechanism to block EPA rules costing over $1 billion — the category covering most major power-plant pollution rules — by having the Energy Department veto rules that raise energy prices or hurt fuel diversity. The public cost would be continued pollution exposure that the rules would have reduced.

industries.industry: Electric utilities and power plant operators
industries.note: Utilities facing expensive compliance with EPA emissions rules would benefit from the bill's block mechanism, though the bill also requires analysis of reliability and fuel-diversity impacts they care about. Consumers would bear any continued pollution and health costs if rules were blocked.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and other large energy consumers
industries.note: The bill explicitly requires the independent analysis to consider energy price increases for manufacturers and small businesses, and its veto could hold down compliance costs passed through as higher prices. The same blocked rules would have delivered health and environmental benefits to the public.

EPA rules that shift the generation mix toward cleaner sources drive demand for renewables; a mechanism to block those rules on cost or fuel-diversity grounds would remove that driver. The bill's fuel-diversity language could also be read to protect incumbent fossil generation.
